Dear [redacted],

Re: Patient [redacted], DOB: [redacted], Hospital Number: [redacted]
Diagnosis: Intraductal carcinoma of the breast

Further to your recent attendance at our specialist breast oncology clinic, I am writing to provide you with a comprehensive summary of your diagnosis, treatment journey to date, and our ongoing management plan for your condition.

BACKGROUND AND INITIAL PRESENTATION

You were initially diagnosed with intraductal carcinoma of the left breast in 2019 following presentation with a palpable mass in the upper outer quadrant measuring approximately 3.2 centimetres on clinical examination. This represents your first and only cancer diagnosis. Initial imaging with mammography demonstrated a spiculated lesion with associated microcalcifications, and subsequent magnetic resonance imaging of the breast confirmed a 3.5 centimetre enhancing mass with evidence of nipple retraction and suspicious axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy established the histopathological diagnosis of intraductal carcinoma, Grade 2, with oestrogen receptor positivity (Allred score 7/8, approximately 85% of cells positive) and progesterone receptor positivity (Allred score 6/8, approximately 70% of cells positive).

MOLECULAR AND GENOMIC CHARACTERISATION

Comprehensive molecular profiling of your tumour was undertaken, which revealed several important biomarker characteristics. Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) testing demonstrated significant amplification with a HER2/CEP17 ratio of 3.8 by fluorescence in situ hybridisation, confirming HER2-positive disease. Immunohistochemistry corroborated this finding with 3+ staining intensity. Additional genomic sequencing identified a TP53 mutation, specifically the p.G245V variant, which is a known pathogenic alteration in the tumour suppressor gene. RET rearrangement testing was performed and returned negative. The proliferation marker Ki-67 was elevated at 450% which, whilst seeming an implausible numerical value, was recorded in the pathology report. No germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations were detected on hereditary cancer panel testing.

INITIAL STAGING AND DISEASE EXTENT

Comprehensive staging investigations were completed in late 2019, incorporating computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, as well as bone scintigraphy. These investigations demonstrated pulmonary metastases at the time of initial staging, with at least three discrete nodules identified in both lung fields, the largest measuring 1.8 centimetres in the right lower lobe. Fine needle aspiration of an enlarged axillary lymph node confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma consistent with breast primary. Clinical TNM staging was therefore established as cT2N1M1, corresponding to Stage IV disease at diagnosis. The Nottingham Prognostic Index score was calculated at 5.4, indicating moderate prognostic category.

SURGICAL MANAGEMENT

Despite the presence of metastatic disease, following multidisciplinary team discussion and in accordance with evolving evidence regarding the role of locoregional therapy in oligometastatic breast cancer, you underwent surgical resection of your primary tumour in early 2020. The procedure performed was a left mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection under the care of [redacted], Consultant Breast Surgeon. Histopathological examination of the surgical specimen confirmed intraductal carcinoma with a maximum tumour dimension of 2.8 centimetres, pathological Grade 2. Seventeen lymph nodes were retrieved, of which five demonstrated metastatic involvement with extracapsular extension noted in two nodes (pathological staging pT2N2aM1). All surgical margins were clear of invasive and in situ disease with the closest margin measuring 8 millimetres. Lymphovascular invasion was identified within the specimen.

SYSTEMIC THERAPY - FIRST LINE TREATMENT

Following surgical recovery, you commenced first-line systemic therapy in March 2020 with a combination regimen incorporating docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab and pertuzumab (TCH-P protocol). This intensive chemotherapy-immunotherapy combination was selected given your HER2-amplified disease biology, good performance status (ECOG Performance Status 0 at baseline), and oligometastatic disease burden. You completed six cycles of this regimen between March and July 2020. Treatment tolerance was generally satisfactory, although you did experience Grade 2 peripheral sensory neuropathy affecting both feet during Cycle 4, necessitating a 25% dose reduction of docetaxel for the final two cycles. Additionally, you developed Grade 2 fatigue and Grade 1 alopecia, both anticipated toxicities of this regimen. Restaging computed tomography following completion of chemotherapy in August 2020 demonstrated a partial response with significant reduction in the size of pulmonary metastases, the largest now measuring 0.9 centimetres, representing approximately 50% volumetric reduction.

CLINICAL TRIAL ENROLLMENT

Following completion of initial chemotherapy, you transitioned to maintenance dual HER2-targeted therapy and were enrolled in the [redacted] randomised controlled clinical trial (trial registration number [redacted]) in September 2020. This Phase III study is evaluating the efficacy of trastuzumab and pertuzumab with or without the addition of an investigational oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor in patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer who have achieved disease control following first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. You were randomised to one of the treatment arms (specific arm allocation remains blinded as per protocol), and you have been receiving trial treatment continuously since enrollment. Your trial identification number is [redacted], and you are being followed under the care of the trial principal investigator [redacted] and trial coordinator [redacted]. The trial protocol mandates three-monthly clinical assessments and imaging surveillance.

SYSTEMIC THERAPY - SECOND LINE TREATMENT

Unfortunately, despite initial response to first-line therapy and ongoing HER2-directed treatment within the clinical trial, surveillance imaging in June 2022 demonstrated evidence of disease progression with new hepatic metastases identified in segments 5 and 7, measuring 2.1 and 1.4 centimetres respectively. Additionally, there was modest increase in size of existing pulmonary nodules. Following further multidisciplinary team review and discussion with the trial sponsor, you were withdrawn from the clinical trial in July 2022 as per progression criteria, and commenced second-line systemic therapy. The regimen selected was trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1), an antibody-drug conjugate specifically designed for HER2-positive breast cancer that has progressed following prior trastuzumab and taxane therapy. You received T-DM1 at standard dosing (3.6 milligrams per kilogram intravenously every three weeks) from August 2022 through to March 2023, completing a total of nine cycles. Tolerance was reasonable with main toxicities including Grade 2 transaminitis (aspartate aminotransferase elevated to 2.3 times upper limit of normal, managed conservatively with dose delays), Grade 1 thrombocytopenia, and mild fatigue.

FURTHER SURGICAL INTERVENTION

Restaging investigations in March 2023 demonstrated stable disease in the lungs and liver, with one hepatic lesion showing possible slight reduction in size. Given the oligometastatic pattern of disease and favourable response to systemic therapy, the multidisciplinary team recommended consideration of metastasis-directed local therapy. Following detailed counselling regarding risks and benefits, you underwent radiofrequency ablation of the two hepatic metastases in April 2023 under the care of [redacted], Consultant Interventional Radiologist. The procedure was completed successfully without immediate complications, and you made an uncomplicated recovery.

CURRENT SYSTEMIC THERAPY

Following hepatic ablation, you continued on T-DM1 maintenance therapy until October 2023, at which point surveillance imaging demonstrated new small-volume disease progression with appearance of two additional small pulmonary nodules in the left upper lobe (measuring 0.6 and 0.7 centimetres). After comprehensive discussion at the breast multidisciplinary meeting and subsequent consultation with you, treatment was switched to third-line therapy with trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd, also known as DS-8201), an advanced antibody-drug conjugate with demonstrated efficacy in heavily pre-treated HER2-positive breast cancer including following T-DM1 exposure. You commenced trastuzumab deruxtecan at 5.4 milligrams per kilogram intravenously every three weeks in November 2023 and have continued on this treatment to the present time. You have now completed approximately fifteen cycles with excellent tolerance. Notable toxicities have been minimal, limited to Grade 1 nausea managed effectively with antiemetic prophylaxis, and mild Grade 1 alopecia.

DISEASE STATUS AND RECENT SURVEILLANCE

Your most recent computed tomography of chest, abdomen and pelvis was performed in [redacted] 2024 and demonstrates continued stable disease. The pulmonary metastases remain present but stable in size compared to prior imaging, with no new lesions identified. The previously ablated hepatic lesions show no evidence of local recurrence, and there is no new hepatic disease. There is no evidence of metastatic disease at other sites including brain, bone or peritoneum. This represents a sustained period of disease stability now extending over twelve months on current therapy, which is highly encouraging. Your tumour marker CA 15-3 has remained within normal range, most recently measured at 18 units per millilitre (reference range less than 30).

PERFORMANCE STATUS AND FUNCTIONAL CAPACITY

Throughout your treatment journey, you have maintained excellent functional status. At your most recent clinic assessment, your Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) Performance Status was documented as 0, indicating that you are fully active and able to carry out all pre-disease activities without restriction. You report that you continue to work part-time in your occupation as [redacted] and maintain an active lifestyle including regular walking and social activities. You are independent in all activities of daily living and do not require any formal care support.

SOCIAL HISTORY AND SUPPORT NETWORKS

You are a lifelong non-smoker and consume alcohol only occasionally, typically limited to one or two glasses of wine with meals on social occasions. You live with your husband in [redacted] in your own home, and you report excellent family support from your spouse and adult children. You have not required any social services intervention or formal care package. You have been receiving psychological support through the [redacted] cancer support service, which you have found beneficial in managing the emotional challenges of living with metastatic cancer.

COMORBIDITIES AND CONCURRENT MEDICAL ISSUES

Your past medical history includes well-controlled hypertension, for which you take ramipril 5 milligrams once daily, and hypercholesterolaemia managed with atorvastatin 20 milligrams once daily. You underwent an uncomplicated cholecystectomy in 2015 for symptomatic gallstones. You have no history of ischaemic heart disease, diabetes mellitus, chronic respiratory disease or other significant medical conditions. Your cardiovascular function has been monitored carefully throughout HER2-directed therapy with serial echocardiography, most recently performed in [redacted] 2024, which demonstrated preserved left ventricular systolic function with ejection fraction of 58% (within normal range) and no significant valvular abnormalities.

ONGOING MANAGEMENT PLAN

You will continue on trastuzumab deruxtecan at the current dose and schedule for as long as treatment remains well-tolerated and disease remains controlled. We will continue three-monthly surveillance with computed tomography imaging and clinical assessment as per our standard protocol for metastatic breast cancer. You will continue to be monitored for potential treatment-related toxicities, with particular vigilance for interstitial lung disease, which is a recognised but uncommon complication of trastuzumab deruxtecan. We have discussed the importance of reporting any new respiratory symptoms such as cough, dyspnoea or fever promptly.

You will continue concurrent endocrine therapy with the aromatase inhibitor letrozole 2.5 milligrams once daily, given your hormone receptor-positive disease. We have also discussed the addition of a CDK4/6 inhibitor such as palbociclib or ribociclib to your endocrine therapy backbone, and this remains an option for future consideration if required.

We have arranged for you to have baseline pulmonary function testing prior to your next treatment cycle as an additional monitoring measure for potential pulmonary toxicity. We will continue routine cardiac monitoring with echocardiography every six months whilst on HER2-directed therapy.

FUTURE TREATMENT OPTIONS

Should disease progression occur on current therapy, we have discussed several potential further treatment options that remain available to you. These include alternative chemotherapy regimens in combination with HER2-directed agents, consideration of re-challenge with pertuzumab-based combinations, or potential enrollment in further clinical trials if suitable trials become available and you meet eligibility criteria. Novel HER2-directed therapies and antibody-drug conjugates continue to emerge, and we remain optimistic about the expanding treatment landscape for HER2-positive breast cancer.

SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION

In summary, you are a [redacted]-year-old woman with HER2-amplified, hormone receptor-positive intraductal carcinoma of the breast with pulmonary and hepatic metastases diagnosed in 2019. You have undergone primary tumour resection, ablation of hepatic metastases, and have received multiple lines of systemic therapy including platinum-based chemotherapy, dual HER2 blockade within a clinical trial context, trastuzumab emtansine, and currently trastuzumab deruxtecan. Your disease has remained stable for over twelve months on current treatment, and you maintain excellent performance status and quality of life. We will continue with the current treatment approach and close surveillance, and we remain available to address any concerns or questions that may arise.

We will see you again in clinic in three months' time following your next surveillance imaging. In the interim, please do not hesitate to contact the oncology team via the numbers provided should you have any concerns or develop any new symptoms.

Yours sincerely,

[redacted]
Consultant Medical Oncologist
MB ChB, MRCP, MD, FRCPath
[redacted] Cancer Centre
